report: Day one of the European paper account, 9 November 2026. The trader made no trades. Equity stays at 1000 euros, all in cash. The day result is zero and the total result is zero. No orders were sent, so there were no fills, no costs and no rejections. Custody cost was zero. Reconcile is consistent and there are no warnings. What moved: crude fell about 3.6 percent after Trump ruled out new Iran strikes. Gold, copper and European indices rose on a US-China truce extension. US CPI is still pending. Why no trade: in oil and gas, the Iran premium is fading and the ENI target raise looked too weak. In gold miners, the rally looked like a continuation that is already priced in, and UK names are costly to trade. In chips, there was only aggregator news, plus an unnamed BofA downgrade and the Nvidia CEO probe. In pharma, Novartis faces an FDA safety probe and the Sanofi news looked stale. In copper and uranium, the move was a continuation with CPI risk ahead. There are no open positions, so there are no exit dates or stops to track. Staying flat cost nothing today. But one quiet day says nothing about skill. We cannot yet tell good caution from missed chances.
questions: The trader rejected every theme partly because the moves were 'continuations already priced in'. What concrete test should separate a priced-in continuation from a fresh, tradable catalyst, so this judgement is not just a habit of staying flat?

The rule is that the expected move must be well above twice the entry cost. Should we write down the round-trip cost per name (for example about 0.9% for IFX.DE, ENI.MI, BESI.AS, BAYN.DE, higher for UK names) so the trader checks a number instead of an impression?

Several reasons rest on aggregator-sourced or unconfirmed items, such as the unnamed BofA chip downgrade. Should the trader be allowed to use unconfirmed news as a reason not to trade, when it is not allowed as a reason to trade?
